extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and mathematicians interested in inequalities, classical proofs, and problem-solving techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material gives theorems, proof strategies, and technical prerequisites for proving and applying classical inequalities and related results (AM-GM, Cauchy, p-adic/valuation methods, Chebyshev, Pólya) and their applications to polynomials, graph theory, and dissection problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic–Geometric Mean (AM–GM) inequality (standard induction scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive numbers a1, ..., an, the geometric mean ≤ arithmetic mean. The text proves AM–GM by base case n = 2 and two-step induction: (A) P(n) ⇒ P(n−1); (B) P(n) and P(2) ⇒ P(2n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case: a1 a2 ≤ ((a1 + a2)/2)^2 follows from (a1 − a2)^2 ≥ 0. For (A) set A = (∏_{k=1}^{n−1} ak)^{1/(n−1)} and manipulate to deduce ∏_{k=1}^{n−1} ak ≤ ( (∑_{k=1}^{n−1} ak)/(n−1) )^{n−1}. For (B) apply P(n) to the two n-tuples formed by first and second halves and use P(2). Equality condition: all ai equal. Also note: apply to reciprocals to get harmonic ≤ geometric. (This entry includes the explicit two-step induction scheme and equality conditions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted AM–GM (Alzer's proof and conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive numbers a1,...,an and positive weights p1,...,pn with ∑ pi = 1, the weighted geometric mean ∏ a_i^{p_i} ≤ ∑ p_i a_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alzer's proof uses monotonicity and integral representations: choose k with a_k ≤ G ≤ a_{k+1} (where G is the weighted geometric mean) and write integrals of the form ∑ p_i (a_i/G)^{1/(G^{-1} t - 1)} dt to show A/G − 1 ≥ log(∏ a_i^{p_i}) − log G = 0, hence A ≥ G. Equality: all a_i equal. (The exposition shows how to pass from integrals to logarithmic expression and deduce the inequality.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Laguerre root-location bound (for polynomials with all real roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all roots of polynomial x^n + a_{n−1} x^{n−1} + ... + a_0 are real, then each root y lies in the interval with endpoints −a_{n−1}/n ± ( (n−1)/n ) * sqrt(a_{n−1}^2 − (2n)/(n−1) a_{n−2} ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: write polynomial as (x−y)∏(x−y_i), compare coefficients to express a_{n−1}, a_{n−2} in terms of y and other roots, apply Cauchy (on vectors of other roots and ones) to bound (a_{n−1} + y)^2 and derive the quadratic inequality in y whose roots give the stated bounds. (The statement and derivation prescribe the exact coefficient manipulations and use of Cauchy to produce the interval.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangential triangle/rectangle formulas and Erdős–Gallai bounds for real-root polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: For a real polynomial f of degree n≥2 with f(x)>0 on (−1,1) and f(−1)=f(1)=0, define area A = ∫_{−1}^{1} f(x) dx, tangential triangle area T (intersection of tangents at −1 and 1), and R = 2 f(b) where b is maximum point. For polynomials with only real roots, 2/3 T ≤ A ≤ 2/3 R, equality holds only for n = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute T via derivatives: T = 2 f'(1) f'(−1) / (f'(1) − f'(−1)) (and T = 0 if both derivatives are zero). For general f(x) = (1−x^2)∏(α_i − x)∏(β_j + x) with α_i,β_j ≥ 1, apply AM–GM to combine mirrored integrals and deduce lower bounds for A in terms of products (α_i^2 − 1)(β_j^2 − 1). Then relate f'(±1) to α_i,β_j and apply harmonic–geometric mean to reach A ≥ 2/3 T. Equality case analysis is by checking when all intermediate inequalities are equalities (forces n=2). (This entry records the precise formula (2) and the chain of inequalities used.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mantel/Turán theorem specialized (triangle-free graphs) and proof criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For a triangle-free graph G on n vertices, |E| ≤ n^2/4; equality occurs only when n is even and G is the complete bipartite graph K_{n/2,n/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First proof (Mantel): denote degrees d_i; since no triangles, for each edge ij we have d_i + d_j ≤ n. Sum over edges to get n|E| ≥ ∑ d_i^2; apply Cauchy to obtain n|E| ≥ (∑ d_i)^2 / n = 4|E|^2/n leading to |E| ≤ n^2/4. Equality analysis: all degrees equal n/2 and G must be K_{n/2,n/2}. Second (folklore) proof: let α be size of maximum independent set, β = n − α. Neighbors of any vertex form independent set so d_i ≤ α; counting edges via vertices in B=V ackslash A gives |E| ≤ ∑_{i∈B} d_i ≤ αβ ≤ ((α+β)/2)^2 = n^2/4 via AM–GM. (This entry captures the degree-counting constraints, two proof routes, and equality characterization.)

rubrics_metrics.name: d'Alembert's lemma (Argand's inequality) and prerequisites for fundamental theorem of algebra proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: If p(a) ≠ 0 for polynomial p, then every disk around a contains an interior point b with |p(b)| < |p(a)|. Prerequisites used: (A) polynomials are continuous, (B) any complex number of absolute value 1 has m-th roots, (C) Cauchy's minimum principle: continuous real-valued functions on a compact set assume a minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: expand p(a+w) as p(a) + c w^m(1 + r(w)) where m is minimal index with nonzero coefficient; choose ζ an m-th root of −p(a)/c |p(a)/c| (unit modulus) and set w0 = ε ζ with ε small enough so that |c w0^m| < |p(a)| and |r(w0)| < 1; use triangle inequality to show |p(a+w0)| < |p(a)|. Then, use growth of |p(z)| at infinity and Cauchy's minimum principle to deduce that minimum of |p| on a large disk interior must be zero, hence p has a root. (This entry lists the exact algebraic factorization step (1) and the choice of parameters and m-th root argument.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and key properties of non-Archimedean (real) valuations (and p-adic example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-Archimedean valuation v: K → R_{≥0} (or into an ordered abelian group with 0 adjoined) satisfies (i) v(x)=0 iff x=0, (ii) v(xy)=v(x)v(y), (iii') v(x+y) ≤ max{v(x),v(y)}. Consequence: (iv) if v(x) ≠ v(y) then v(x+y) = max{v(x),v(y)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollaries: v(1)=1, v(−1)=1, v(−x)=v(x), v(x^{-1}) = v(x)^{-1}. Example: p-adic valuation on Q: express r = p^k a/b with a,b coprime to p then |r|_p = p^{−k}; this satisfies the stronger non-Archimedean inequality and (iv). The text notes Ostrowski's theorem: all nontrivial real non-Archimedean valuations of Q are p-adic (up to powers). (This entry includes the necessary properties used later in coloring arguments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monsky's theorem proof ingredients and coloring/valuation rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsky's theorem: A square cannot be dissected into an odd number of triangles of equal area. Proof uses a valuation v with v(1/2) > 1 (extended suitably from Q to R), a 3-coloring of the plane based on which of v(x), v(y), v(1) is maximal for triple (x,y,1), and combinatorial counting (Sperner-style) to force an odd number of 'rainbow' triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coloring rule: a point (x,y) is blue if v(x) ≥ v(y), v(x) ≥ v(1); green if v(x) < v(y), v(y) ≥ v(1); red if v(x) < v(1), v(y) < v(1). Lemma: for blue,green,red points p_b,p_g,p_r, the determinant det([[x_b,y_b,1],[x_g,y_g,1],[x_r,y_r,1]]) has v-value ≥ 1; hence any rainbow triangle has area whose v-value > 1 and cannot equal 1/n for odd n (since v(1/n)=1 for odd n while v(1/2)>1 implies v(±2/n) < 1 contradicting lemma). Combinatorial lemma: in any planar dissection, count red–blue segments on triangle boundaries — boundary contributes odd number => odd number of rainbow triangles. Existence of required valuation: exhibited via valuation rings and Zorn's lemma (maximal subring not containing 1/2), yielding valuation with v(1/2)>1. (This entry contains the precise coloring rule, determinant lemma, area/valuation contradiction, and the Sperner-type counting step.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant valuation lemma (Monsky intermediate technical criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any blue point p_b=(x_b,y_b), green p_g=(x_g,y_g), red p_r=(x_r,y_r) with coloring defined by valuation v, the v-value of the determinant of the 3×3 matrix with rows (x,y,1) is at least 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: determinant expands into six terms; the main diagonal term x_b y_g 1 has v ≥ 1 because each diagonal entry is maximal in its row; each other summand involves at least one entry below the diagonal with strictly smaller v and at least one above with no larger v, so their v-values are strictly smaller; then non-Archimedean property (iv) gives v(det)=v(main diagonal) ≥ 1. Consequence: rainbow triangle area (half that determinant) has v-value ≥ v(1/2)^{-1} * 1 > 1, so cannot equal rational 1/n for odd n (since v(1/n)=1). (This entry captures the algebraic determinant comparison argument and its implications.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner-style counting lemma for dissections (Monsky)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any finite triangulation/dissection of the unit square, there is an odd number of rainbow triangles (triangles with vertices of all three colors), hence at least one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define red–blue segments (edge endpoints colored red and blue). Observations: (A) bottom side of square has an odd number of red–blue segments (endpoints colored red and blue), other boundary sides have none; (B) any non-rainbow triangle contributes an even number (0 or 2) of red–blue boundary segments, while a rainbow triangle contributes an odd number (1 or 3). Counting red–blue segments over all triangle boundaries: interior segments counted twice, boundary segments once; since boundary count is odd, total is odd, forcing an odd number of rainbow triangles. (This entry states the counting invariant and parity argument.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension/existence of valuations via valuation rings and Zorn's lemma (construction criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a valuation on R with v(1/2) > 1, construct a maximal subring B ⊂ R that does not contain 1/2; such a B is a valuation ring and induces a valuation into an ordered abelian group G (via K×/U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key facts: for a valuation v, its valuation ring R_v = {x: v(x) ≤ 1}, units U = {x: v(x)=1}, and K = R_v ∪ R_v^{-1}. Conversely any proper subring R with K = R ∪ R^{-1} arises from a valuation. Existence: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal subring B not containing 1/2; maximality forces B to be a valuation ring (proof by contradiction: adjoining α outside B∪B^{-1} would yield contradiction via polynomial representations and minimality arguments), hence yields desired valuation with v(1/2)>1. (This entry records both the algebraic characterization and the Zorn-based existence strategy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev–type extremal criterion for polynomials (Chebyshev theorem and corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chebyshev's theorem: For real polynomial p(x) of degree n with leading coefficient 1, max_{−1≤x≤1} |p(x)| ≥ 1/2^{n−1}. Corollary: If |p(x)| ≤ 2 on [a,b] then b − a ≤ 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea of corollary: scale variable to map [a,b] to [−1,1], obtain q(y) with leading coefficient ( (b−a)/2 )^n, then apply Chebyshev lower bound to deduce 2 ≥ ( (b−a)/2 )^n (1/2^{n−1}) = 2 ( (b−a)/4 )^n, hence b−a ≤ 4. (This entry records the exact extremal bound and the scaling trick used to deduce interval-length restrictions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya projection length theorem and reduction to real-root polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex polynomial f(z) = z^n + b_{n−1} z^{n−1} + ... + b_0 (leading coefficient 1), set C = {z ∈ C : |f(z)| ≤ 2}. The orthogonal projection of C onto any line has total length ≤ 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction: rotate plane so line is real axis. If z = x + i y ∈ C, then for roots c_k = a_k + i b_k, we have |x − a_k| ≤ |z − c_k| so |p(x)| = ∏ |x − a_k| ≤ ∏ |z − c_k| = |f(z)| ≤ 2, hence projection R ⊆ P = {x ∈ R : |p(x)| ≤ 2} where p(x) = ∏ (x − a_k) is a real polynomial with all roots real. Apply Theorem 2 (cover P by intervals of total length ≤ 4 via Chebyshev/Chebyshev-derived construction). Pólya's trick: if P consists of several disjoint intervals, construct another degree-n polynomial p with leading coeff 1 whose small-level set is a single interval whose length at least the sum of lengths of P's components, then apply Chebyshev corollary to bound total length ≤ 4. (This entry gives the reduction step and overall strategy to reach the projection-length bound.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial-interval splitting and shifting construction (Pólya technical device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given p(x) = q(x) r(x) with roots split between disjoint components of P = {x : |p(x)| ≤ 2}, shift the factor q by the gap distance d between two adjacent components to form p1(x) = q(x + d) r(x); this construction increases |p| on earlier intervals so that the union of small-level sets for suitable choices can be merged into a single interval whose length at least sum of original components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete step: when the rightmost component contains m < n roots b_i, and the previous component lies at distance d, write p = q r with q having roots in rightmost component and r the remaining roots; then p1(x)=q(x+d) r(x) satisfies |q(x+d)| < |q(x)| for x in left components, so |p1(x)| < |p(x)| and one can construct a polynomial p of degree n with leading coefficient 1 such that its small-level set 'P covers the union of the original disjoint intervals; then apply Chebyshev corollary to bound total length ≤ 4. (This entry records the shifting idea and its role in Pólya's argument.)
